docs.title: Transport Lab
docs.text:
A learning fork

This is a slop fork for me to learn about different transport strategies.

What happens between “send this message” and “the other machine can use it”? This fork explores that question with a small, inspectable sender/receiver benchmark, then connects those ideas to distributed GPU systems.

Start with KCP, ENet, TCP and UDP, look at the measured results, or jump to the hardware that moves data between GPUs.

docs.title: What is here?
docs.text:
Question Read Why can reliable delivery make a message late? Transport fundamentals How do we reproduce a bad network? Benchmark and results Can AI propose better transport algorithms? The iteration workflow Does GPU communication still use packets? From tensors to packets What actually handles acknowledgements and congestion? Network cards and switches

The benchmark runs real processes through an emulated network. The GPU chapters explain established designs; we have not benchmarked GPUs or RDMA hardware in this repository.

docs.title: The first useful finding
docs.text:
In a short workload with 50 ms of delay in each direction, KCP's starting congestion window caused a large sender backlog. An experimental initial window of ten segments reduced pooled p95 delivery latency from 1,631.6 ms to 61.3 ms, with about 11% more transmitted traffic. That is evidence about this configuration and workload, not a universal protocol ranking.

Explore the interactive report Read the measurement limits

The report contains 144 development and validation trials from October 10, 2026. Six additional duplication/reordering trials checked correctness. See the experiment ledger for provenance and decisions.

docs.title: Benchmark and results
docs.text:
We run a sender and receiver through Linux network namespaces, with tc netem introducing impairments in both directions:

sender process → virtual link → router → virtual link → receiver process
                                 ↑
                         delay, loss, rate limit

This exercises real sockets and protocol implementations. The router is isolated from the host's normal network interfaces. Netem supports UDP and TCP, which is why it fits this comparison; Toxiproxy is a TCP proxy and would not directly exercise the UDP transports. See the netem manual.

docs.title: Reproduce a run
docs.text:
Run from a Linux checkout with root privileges for network namespace setup:

sudo apt-get install build-essential libenet-dev iproute2 ethtool iputils-ping pkg-config
sudo python3 benchmarks/network/run.py \
  --out /var/tmp/transport-smoke \
  --profiles clean --count 50 --repeats 1 --candidates kcp_iw10
PEER_BINARY=/var/tmp/transport-smoke/peer \
  python3 -m unittest discover -s benchmarks/network -p 'test_*.py'

Always choose a fresh output directory. For full development and validation runs, use the commands in the iteration guide. The canonical benchmark README documents exact configuration, installation and outputs.

docs.title: What stays fixed?
docs.text:
The transport-v2 workload sends 500 messages of 256 bytes at 100 messages/second, followed by a four-second drain. That is 204.8 kbit/s of offered application payload. Five controls—UDP, KCP, KCP with congestion control disabled, ENet and TCP—run alongside a registered candidate.

Latency is measured from scheduled send time to application delivery, so sender queueing counts. All endpoints share the host's monotonic clock. The deadline is 100 ms. Delivery and deadline percentages use all offered messages as the denominator; latency percentiles include only messages delivered within the observation window. A missing message can still be queued rather than permanently lost.

Both endpoint TX counters count traffic including acknowledgements and retries. These are interface counters in an emulated network, not physical-wire byte measurements.

Development profile Impairment in each direction Clean 2 ms delay Distant 50 ms delay, approximately 100 ms base RTT Jitter/loss 50 ms delay, 20 ms jitter, 1% random loss Burst loss 20 ms delay and alternating good/bad loss states Constrained 20 ms delay, 128 kbit/s—below the offered payload rate Outage 20 ms delay with roughly two seconds of complete loss

Separate profiles test duplication/reordering and different validation conditions. See suite.json for exact parameters.

docs.title: Why was KCP so slow on the distant link?
docs.text:
The trace showed a small initial congestion window and a growing sender backlog. This short workload includes startup: there is no warm-up. The kcp_iw10 candidate starts with ten segments instead of one and otherwise keeps the built-in congestion controller.

Variant Pooled p95 latency Largest observed sender queue KCP baseline 1,631.6 ms 163 segments KCP, congestion control disabled 61.1 ms 1 segment KCP, initial window ten 61.3 ms 2 segments

The initial-window candidate transmitted about 11% more traffic than the baseline in this profile. This is a configuration experiment, not a newly invented congestion-control algorithm. It remains experimental: in development jitter/loss trials, only 6.1% of its offered messages met the deadline and 86.3% arrived within the observation window.

docs.title: Why include UDP?
docs.text:
During the outage trials, UDP delivered 893 of 1,500 offered messages. Its surviving messages could arrive quickly because there was no recovery queue. Reporting only their latency would hide the missing 607 messages.

The dedicated duplication/reordering check recorded 10 duplicate UDP arrivals and 17 reordered first arrivals. All five reliable variants delivered 100/100 messages once and in order in that check.

Open the interactive results

The report preserves the original 144 development/validation trials and browser controls. The experiment ledger records the additional six correctness trials, candidate hash, traffic tradeoffs and retained artifact locations. Documentation publication did not rerun these experiments.

docs.title: What the results do not establish
docs.text:
The October 10, 2026 pilot used three repeats and three concurrent trials sharing CPU resources; the runner defaults to serial execution. Random loss was unseeded: the settings are reproducible, exact packet outcomes are not. Three repeats do not establish statistical confidence.

We have not measured competing-flow fairness, CPU/memory cost, encrypted transports, or real GPU/RDMA performance. The short test includes startup and is not a sustained-throughput benchmark. Historical v1 and v2 results use different evaluator rules and should not be directly ranked against each other.

docs.title: From GPU tensors to network packets
docs.text: Distributed GPU communication still faces loss, congestion and delayed packets. Specialised hardware changes where much of the work happens; it does not make those problems disappear.

docs.title: Three different decisions
docs.text:
Layer Question Examples Collective algorithm Which GPU sends which tensor chunks to whom? Ring/tree all-reduce, all-gather, all-to-all Transport How are chunks delivered and losses recovered? TCP; reliable RDMA over InfiniBand or RoCE Interconnect How do bits travel between devices? NVLink, PCIe, Ethernet, InfiniBand

NCCL coordinates collective communication on NVIDIA GPUs. For example, all-reduce can sum contributions from multiple GPUs and return the result to each participant. Operations are enqueued on CUDA streams: the application must respect completion and memory-ordering requirements before using results. NCCL documentation

docs.title: Inside a server
docs.text: Where topology and peer access support it, GPUs can access each other's memory over NVLink or PCIe. NVSwitch provides switching for NVLink-connected GPUs; it is different from an Ethernet switch. Some larger systems extend NVLink connectivity across a rack, so the server boundary is not a universal dividing line. NVIDIA NVLink

docs.title: Across a network
docs.text:
A common high-performance path is GPUDirect RDMA:

GPU A memory → RDMA network card → switches → RDMA network card → GPU B memory

The network adapter can read or write GPU memory without staging the payload in CPU memory. The CPU/driver still helps establish mappings and connections and may submit communication work. “Direct” does not mean packets bypass switches or that CPU involvement is always zero. GPUDirect RDMA documentation

Where direct GPU memory access or RDMA is unavailable, communication may use host-memory staging and TCP sockets. The actual path depends on topology, drivers, network plugins and configuration; an advertised GPU model alone does not establish which path a job uses. NCCL troubleshooting

docs.title: InfiniBand, RoCE and UDP
docs.text:
InfiniBand is a specialised networking architecture with RDMA support. RoCE means RDMA over Converged Ethernet. RoCEv2 wraps its RDMA transport packets in UDP/IP, allowing routing across IP networks.

UDP is the envelope. A reliable RDMA connection adds its own sequencing, acknowledgements and recovery; it does not ask training code to accept missing tensor bytes. RDMA also has unreliable modes, so “RDMA” alone is not a delivery guarantee. NVIDIA RoCE documentation and RDMA transport modes

This resembles KCP-over-UDP at one level: both can add reliability above UDP. The implementation and application interface differ substantially. KCP is software driven by the application; an RDMA adapter can perform transport processing and direct memory placement in hardware.

docs.title: Why congestion matters on a wired cluster
docs.text:
Imagine many GPUs finishing computation together and sending to one destination. The receiver's link has a finite rate. Switch queues grow when incoming traffic exceeds outgoing capacity, even with perfect cables. A large queue increases latency; exhausted buffers can cause drops.

A collective can be delayed by one slow participant or transfer. That makes communication scheduling, topology, congestion control and tail latency relevant to overall compute utilisation. Our network hardware chapter follows the feedback loop that tells senders to slow down.

Scope of our experiment

Our socket/netem benchmark explores reliability, queues and deadlines. It does not emulate RDMA adapter internals, NVLink, switch credit systems or GPU memory synchronisation. Its KCP rankings cannot be transferred directly to a GPU cluster.

docs.title: The hardware that handles GPU networking
docs.text: The main pieces are RDMA-capable network adapters in the servers and switches connecting those adapters. The adapters handle transport endpoints and memory access. The switches forward packets and help control congestion.

docs.title: What would you actually find in a rack?
docs.text:
Component Example Job RDMA network adapter NVIDIA/Mellanox ConnectX Move data between memory and the network; process RDMA transport Ethernet switch NVIDIA Spectrum or another suitable data-centre Ethernet switch Forward Ethernet traffic and provide queue/congestion controls for RoCE InfiniBand switch NVIDIA Quantum Forward InfiniBand traffic with its fabric mechanisms DPU NVIDIA BlueField Combine networking acceleration with programmable processing for infrastructure services GPU interconnect switch NVSwitch Connect GPUs over NVLink; a separate role from Ethernet/InfiniBand networking

An InfiniBand adapter is often called an HCA, or host channel adapter. A RoCE adapter is often called an RNIC, an RDMA network interface controller. “SuperNIC” is vendor terminology for adapters aimed at accelerated computing; it is not a separate wire protocol. A DPU is not required for basic RDMA.

Product references: ConnectX adapters, Spectrum Ethernet, Quantum InfiniBand, BlueField, NVLink/NVSwitch. These are examples, not requirements or a purchasing recommendation; features vary by device and generation.

docs.title: Follow one RDMA write
docs.text:
Suppose GPU A has a tensor to place in GPU B's memory.

  1. Prepare memory. Software registers/maps the buffers and grants the adapter access. The receiver supplies an authorised destination address and access key.
  2. Submit work. Software places a descriptor on a send queue: source, destination and length. A notification, often called a doorbell, tells the adapter to process queued work.
  3. Make packets. The adapter reads source memory using DMA, divides the transfer into packets and adds transport headers and sequence information.
  4. Deliver and recover. On a reliable connection, adapters track acknowledgements and retry missing data. A permanent failure eventually produces an error, not guaranteed delivery.
  5. Place data. The receiving adapter checks permissions and writes into the registered destination. Completion records report work status; the application still needs the correct synchronisation before using the data.

The associated send/receive queues are called a queue pair. A completion queue reports completed operations. These let software submit transfers rather than process every packet itself. NVIDIA RDMA programming manual

With GPUDirect RDMA, those buffers can be in GPU memory, subject to supported topology and mappings. Bypassing CPU payload copies does not remove memory-ordering requirements. GPUDirect RDMA

docs.title: What makes the adapter different from a normal network card?
docs.text:
Ordinary NICs already offload jobs such as checksums and segmentation. An RDMA adapter additionally maintains transport and memory-access state: queues, registered memory permissions, sequence numbers, acknowledgements and retransmission machinery. Dedicated logic, firmware and sometimes programmable processors do work that a conventional socket transport would largely perform in the host networking stack.

The advantage is reduced CPU work and fewer payload copies at high data rates. It does not eliminate protocol overhead, finite buffers or contention. ConnectX architecture and capabilities

docs.title: How switches and cards cooperate on congestion
docs.text:
For a common RoCE congestion-control design, the loop looks like this:

Switch queue grows
        ↓
Switch marks passing packets: congestion experienced (ECN)
        ↓
Receiver adapter sends a congestion notification (CNP)
        ↓
Sender adapter reduces its sending rate
        ↓
Queue drains; sender later probes for available capacity

DCQCN is one algorithm for adjusting the sender's rate using that feedback. This is a control algorithm with parameters and tradeoffs, even though it runs on a network device.

Priority Flow Control (PFC) is a different mechanism: a congested device can ask its immediate upstream neighbour to temporarily pause a traffic priority. It can prevent buffer overflow but can also spread stalls upstream. It is not end-to-end retransmission or a substitute for a good congestion controller. RoCE deployments differ; PFC is not universally required by the protocol. RoCE congestion controls and NVIDIA deployment without PFC

InfiniBand uses link-level credits to keep a transmitter within the next hop's advertised buffering capacity. It also has end-to-end congestion controls. Such flow control avoids certain drops, but blocked links and congestion can still delay useful work. InfiniBand architecture overview

docs.title: Can we experiment with these algorithms?
docs.text:
Yes, but the available control points depend on hardware. Some NVIDIA devices expose programmable congestion-control infrastructure, including algorithms based on explicit congestion feedback and round-trip-time measurements. This is more constrained than compiling an arbitrary C library on the host. NVIDIA congestion-control infrastructure

For this repository, the practical progression is to study sender/receiver control algorithms, add multi-sender workloads, then test suitable candidates on real RDMA equipment. Evidence should include total exchange completion time, queue/congestion counters, retries and fairness. None of that hardware validation has been performed here yet.

docs.title: Iterating on AI-generated algorithms
docs.text: The approach borrows from Squeeze: keep the interface and workload common, preserve controls, and let a candidate earn its claims through measurements. An AI-generated explanation is a hypothesis, not evidence.

docs.title: One bounded experiment
docs.text:
1. Write the hypothesis and expected cost before inspecting results.
  2. Add a new candidate file and registry entry; preserve the baseline.
  3. Run correctness checks and a small sender/receiver smoke test.
  4. Evaluate against every control on the same development workload.
  5. Freeze the candidate, run validation, and record the decision, hashes and artifacts—including unsuccessful results.

The interface is deliberately small:

#include "ikcp.h"
int configure_candidate(ikcpcb *kcp);

A candidate can change startup state or install a congestion controller through IKCPOPS and ikcp_setcc. Keep changes inside its candidate source. The first example, kcp_iw10, changes the initial window and corresponding byte state; it is a configuration candidate.

Read the canonical iteration protocol and local agent rules before changing candidate code.

docs.title: Run and compare
docs.text:
With just installed, from the repository root:

just candidates
just smoke /var/tmp/transport-smoke-new
just benchmark /var/tmp/transport-development-new kcp_iw10
just validate /var/tmp/transport-validation-new kcp_iw10
just compare /var/tmp/transport-development-new kcp_iw10

Keep suite.json, peer.c, metrics.py and run.py fixed during an experiment. An evaluator correction requires a versioned change and fresh control runs. Do not let a candidate inspect profile names, drop hard messages to improve percentiles, or weaken payload checks.

Review generated C before running it: network namespaces isolate network interfaces, not arbitrary code's filesystem access.

docs.title: What counts as better?
docs.text:
Compare delivery and deadline success first, then traffic and the latency distribution. Inspect each profile and repeat. A faster result that uses much more traffic may be an undesirable tradeoff; turning off congestion control also raises fairness questions this harness cannot answer yet.

The comparison tool excludes UDP from reliable-candidate rankings and leaves decisions for review. There is no automatic promotion or endless search. Public validation profiles stop being independent evidence once repeatedly used for tuning.

docs.title: Extending the idea to GPUs
docs.text:
A useful future workload would make eight senders finish a tensor exchange before the next compute step can start. Measure total completion time, slowest-participant latency, useful bandwidth and fairness under competing flows. Ring all-reduce and all-to-all would add communication patterns that a single sender/receiver does not capture.

Those are proposed experiments, not implemented GPU results. Actual RDMA testing needs suitable hardware and measurements of its queues and congestion signals. See GPU transport.

docs.title: Building and publishing this documentation
docs.text: The site uses MkDocs Material. Its source is in docs/, with navigation in mkdocs.yml and pinned top-level documentation dependencies in requirements-docs.txt.

docs.title: Local preview and checks
docs.text:
From the repository root:

python3 -m venv .venv-docs
.venv-docs/bin/pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
.venv-docs/bin/mkdocs build --strict
.venv-docs/bin/mkdocs serve

Open the local address printed by MkDocs. The generated site/ directory and virtual environment are ignored by Git. The strict build rejects documentation warnings, including unresolved internal page links.

The report at docs/reports/transport-v2.html is a frozen copy of the October 10, 2026 benchmark artifact. It works without external assets. Editing prose or rebuilding the site does not regenerate or rerun that experiment.

docs.title: GitHub Pages
docs.text:
The public site is georgepearse.github.io/kcp. GitHub Pages serves the root of the gh-pages branch. Publish a reviewed local build with:

.venv-docs/bin/mkdocs gh-deploy --strict

This pushes generated output to gh-pages; it does not merge the source branch. The first publication was made from docs/learning-fork-callout while its source changes remained in a draft PR.

The documentation workflow validates pull requests. Once integrated into the default english-docs branch, source changes there also rebuild and update gh-pages. Because pushes made with the default Actions token do not themselves trigger a Pages build, the workflow explicitly requests one using the Pages API after deploying. Check both the documentation workflow and the Pages deployment before treating an update as live.

Source changes still go through a feature branch and draft PR. Publishing the documentation is separate from promoting any transport candidate.

References: Material publishing guide, GitHub Pages publishing sources, and Pages build API.

docs.title: KCP, ENet, TCP and UDP
docs.text: A transport chooses what delivery promises to make, and how to keep those promises when packets arrive late, disappear, or arrive out of order. Wired networks need these decisions too: a congested switch can run out of buffer space even when every cable works perfectly.

docs.title: What each option promises
docs.text:
Option What the application receives Where the transport runs Plain UDP Separate datagrams, possibly missing, duplicated or reordered OS sockets; no built-in delivery recovery KCP over UDP Reliable, ordered messages in this benchmark C library driven by the application ENet Reliable or unreliable messages, with channels; we select one reliable ordered channel C networking library over UDP TCP Reliable, ordered bytes; the application defines message boundaries Usually the OS networking stack

“Reliable” does not mean delivery is guaranteed before a deadline or through a permanent disconnection. Our reliable variants can still have messages waiting when the measurement window ends.

UDP is the substrate for KCP and ENet in this setup. It is also useful as its own baseline: what latency and delivery do we get without paying for acknowledgements or retries? But it cannot win a reliable-delivery comparison by simply abandoning the difficult messages.

Sources: UDP specification, TCP specification, ENet design, and KCP source.

docs.title: Why a fast link can deliver a message late
docs.text:
Suppose messages 1, 2 and 3 are sent, but the packet containing message 2 disappears. Plain UDP can deliver 1 and 3 immediately. An ordered reliable transport must recover 2 before exposing 3 in that same ordered sequence. The wait is called head-of-line blocking.

There can also be a queue before the first packet leaves. A congestion window limits outstanding unacknowledged data. If the application produces messages faster than the initial window allows, messages wait at the sender. Our distant-link experiment demonstrates this.

These controls have different purposes:

  • Reliability: detect missing data and retransmit it.
  • Flow control: avoid overrunning the receiver.
  • Congestion control: avoid overwhelming the network between the endpoints.
  • Pacing: spread transmissions over time instead of emitting a large burst.

KCP's nc=1 disables its built-in congestion control; it does not disable all receiver/window limits. A faster isolated run with that setting does not establish fair behavior alongside other traffic.

docs.title: Follow a message through this repository
docs.text:
In the endpoint implementation, the application submits data through ikcp_send. Periodic ikcp_update calls advance the protocol. Its output callback sends resulting packets through UDP. The receiver passes incoming packets to ikcp_input and obtains delivered messages with ikcp_recv.

KCP itself does not own the socket or clock. That separation makes this a useful place to experiment with acknowledgement, window and retransmission behavior.

docs.title: Other alternatives worth comparing
docs.text:
Alternative Why it is interesting GameNetworkingSockets Reliable/unreliable messages, encryption and connection features for games QUIC, such as quiche Encrypted transport over UDP; independently ordered streams reduce cross-stream delivery blocking SCTP / usrsctp Message-oriented transport, multiple streams and ordered/unordered delivery SRT Retransmission and latency buffering designed for live media

These overlap in purpose; they are not wire-compatible replacements. They are not yet measured by this harness.

Reading the upstream README

The inherited README includes historical performance claims and simplified TCP comparisons. Modern TCP can selectively acknowledge and recover lost data; it does not generally resend every packet after a loss. Use measured configurations rather than a universal “KCP is faster” percentage. See TCP SACK and RACK loss detection.

docs.title: Stable video capacity on bad networks
docs.text:
The question is how much video we can continuously carry without stalling playback, not how many bytes eventually arrive. This benchmark sweeps video bitrate and confirms the highest passing rates with longer runs.

Explore sustainable bitrate results

docs.title: What “stable” means
docs.text:
The virtual player has a fixed two-second playout offset. Every one-second video segment must be complete by its scheduled playback time. We also reject a run if mean delivery latency grows by more than 250ms between the first ten and last ten segments, even if the buffer has not yet run dry.

No skipped segments, adaptive bitrate or ever-growing buffer can turn a failure into a pass. The report shows deadline failures, accumulated extra stall time and delivery latency over time. Missing segments produce a lower bound on stall time at the observation cutoff.

docs.title: Find a capacity bound
docs.text:
1. Encode actual conveyor footage at six requested H.264 rates: 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 5.5 Mbit/s.
  2. Screen each rate for 30 seconds with TCP, KCP and plain UDP on each network profile.
  3. Test the highest screened pass and next higher rate in two independent 90-second runs.
  4. If the selected rate fails confirmation, step down and test the next lower rate twice.
  5. Report the highest confirmed actual bitrate and any tested failing upper neighbour.

Actual encoded rates include segment/container overhead and differ from encoder targets. A result is a tested bound, not proof of an exact continuous maximum or a guarantee for arbitrary outages.

docs.title: The bad networks
docs.text:
Both directions have a 5 Mbit/s limit and a 1,000-packet queue:

Profile Additional impairment, each direction Loss and jitter 40ms delay, 10ms normal jitter, 1% independent random loss Burst loss 20ms delay; Gilbert–Elliott bad-state entry1%, exit25%, bad-state loss80%, good-state loss0%

Real sender/receiver processes run in separate Linux namespaces through a netem router. Random loss is unseeded. This exploratory run uses three concurrent isolated trials on one host.

docs.title: Video and transport contract
docs.text:
The five-second conveyor edge fixture is encoded into independently decodable one-second H.264 segments at 1080p/10fps, then repeated. Each source segment is decoded and frame-counted before testing. Every received segment must match its SHA-256 before it can be played. The entire offered timeline stays in the denominator.

TCP uses CUBIC and NODELAY. KCP uses built-in congestion control and128-segment windows; these are baseline settings, not a video-tuned controller. UDP has fragment metadata but no recovery or FEC. Requiring complete segments is more conservative than players that conceal packet damage or recover partial frames.

Media is pre-encoded. This measures transport and a deterministic playback model; it does not run a live GStreamer/RTP/RTSP player or include capture/encoding time. Lower bitrates can reduce visual quality, which this benchmark does not evaluate. QUIC, TLS, production GCS and physical WAN links are not tested here.

docs.title: Measured capacity bounds
docs.text:
The completed run contains 36 × 30-second screens and 20 × 90-second confirmations: 48 minutes of offered video across 56 trials. Every confirmed rate below passed both long repeats.

Network Transport Highest confirmed actual video bitrate Higher tested failure loss_jitter tcp 0.581 Mbit/s 1.152 Mbit/s loss_jitter kcp 0.295 Mbit/s 0.581 Mbit/s loss_jitter udp None demonstrated 0.295 Mbit/s (lowest tested) burst_loss tcp None demonstrated 0.295 Mbit/s (lowest tested) burst_loss kcp None demonstrated 0.295 Mbit/s (lowest tested) burst_loss udp None demonstrated 0.295 Mbit/s (lowest tested)

On the loss/jitter link, TCP passed at 0.581 Mbit/s and KCP at 0.295 Mbit/s. At1.152 Mbit/s, one TCP confirmation delivered all90 segments by their deadlines but still failed because mean latency grew by344ms. Byte delivery or a short run would miss that warning sign.

No transport demonstrated a stable rate on the burst-loss profile at the tested rates, down to0.295 Mbit/s. This does not establish that a lower rate, different buffer budget, FEC or another transport configuration cannot work.

docs.title: Evidence and reproduction
docs.text:
See the frozen benchmark contract and results ledger. All failed trials, arrival records, network counters and source/segment hashes are retained. Raw footage is not in this public site.

The earlier four-second payload pilot is retained separately. It measured short-run delivery and codec sizes; it does not establish sustainable streaming capacity.

docs.title: How much video can the network carry?
docs.text:
Historical short-run pilot

This four-second test does not establish stable streaming capacity. Use the sustained video benchmark for bitrate bounds, playback stalls and latency growth.

This pilot sends actual encoded video bytes through the same kind of isolated Linux sender/router/receiver network used by the small-message benchmark. It measures how much complete video arrives, and how much arrives soon enough for a chosen playback deadline.

Explore the video delivery report

docs.title: Workload
docs.text:
The sources are existing edge-test fixtures: four seconds of conveyor footage and the first four seconds of a Big Buck Bunny clip. The Bunny opening is smooth and low-detail; the conveyor contains textured moving material. These are a small pilot, not a representative video corpus.

Both are encoded at 1920×1080, 10fps, using either H.264 (libx264 veryfast, CRF23, no B frames) or MJPEG (quality 4). Each one-second segment is independently decodable. The settings are not matched for visual quality; this does not measure codec quality or downstream detection accuracy.

Source H.264 encoded bitrate MJPEG encoded bitrate Conveyor 7.357 Mbit/s 12.991 Mbit/s Bunny opening 0.951 Mbit/s 4.993 Mbit/s

These rates include the segment container, before network/protocol overhead. A link needs additional headroom. The large difference between clips shows why resolution and FPS alone do not determine video bandwidth.

docs.title: Network experiment
docs.text:
The suite runs TCP, KCP with built-in congestion control, and best-effort UDP. Each receives the same encoded payload, packet framing and pacing schedule. There are four profiles, each with 20ms delay per direction: 20 Mbit/s, 5 Mbit/s, 5 Mbit/s with 1% random loss, and 1 Mbit/s. Two repeats across all combinations produce 96 trials. Three trials run concurrently on the same host.

Each trial offers four seconds of video over four seconds, then permits three seconds to drain. A segment is complete only when its SHA-256 matches the original. It is on time only if complete within 1.5 seconds of its scheduled release. Every source segment was decoded to ten frames before transmission.

A partly received segment earns byte-delivery credit but no usable-video credit. That is intentionally conservative: a specialised decoder could recover some frames from a damaged stream. It does not mean every UDP/RTP streaming system would lose as much video as this simple no-retry framing.

docs.title: What this tells us about the edge
docs.text:
At these settings, a 5 Mbit/s uplink cannot carry the conveyor's H.264 output in real time even before transport overhead. The Bunny clip fits much more easily. Choosing an appropriate encoding, frame rate or resolution is therefore necessary before tuning transport.

The 20 Mbit/s capacity control distinguishes link saturation from transport startup and window behaviour. KCP uses the existing small-window controller, not a video-tuned configuration. Slow results here do not establish a limit on every possible KCP configuration.

Use the report to compare complete seconds, on-time seconds, received payload and transmitted traffic. Looking at bytes alone can hide scattered losses that prevent reconstruction; looking only at latency of successful deliveries can hide missing video.

docs.title: A concrete loss comparison
docs.text:
For the Bunny H.264 clip on the 5 Mbit/s link with 1% loss, across two repeats:

Transport Complete seconds / 8 offered On-time seconds / 8 offered TCP 8 8 KCP 8 6 UDP 2 2

The clean 20 Mbit/s control delivered all eight conveyor seconds on time with TCP and UDP for both encodings. At 5 Mbit/s, neither encoding delivered any complete conveyor segment within the chosen deadline, regardless of transport. TCP still completed all eight H.264 seconds during the longer observation window: complete delivery and timely playback are different outcomes.

docs.title: Reproduce and inspect
docs.text:
The benchmark README documents dependencies, commands and the fixed workload. The results ledger contains every aggregate comparison and validation details. Source hashes, segment hashes, raw arrivals, network commands and counters are retained with the run.

This is separate from the original transport-v2 benchmark. It uses pre-encoded media, excludes capture/encoding cost, and does not run GStreamer, RTP/RTSP, QUIC, TLS or the production GCS uploader. Random loss is unseeded and two repeats are exploratory. Raw footage is not included in this public documentation.
